```{r load-data}
#| include: false
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Flux data from Block 4
source("scripts/read_hh.R")
dir.create("data/processed", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
cache_file <- "data/processed/all_hh.rds"
if (file.exists(cache_file)) {
  all_hh <- readRDS(cache_file)
} else {
  zips   <- list.files("data/raw", pattern = "\\.zip$", full.names = TRUE)
  all_hh <- bind_rows(lapply(zips, read_hh))
  saveRDS(all_hh, cache_file)
}

# Block 5 datasets
soil   <- read_csv("data/external/soilgrids/soilgrids_my_sites.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
traits <- read_csv("data/external/planttraits/planttraits_my_sites.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

## 3. Greenness and GPP

## 4. My question: soil C:N and light-use efficiency

**Question.** Is the topsoil C:N ratio related to ecosystem light-use
efficiency (LUE) during the peak growing season across my five towers?

**Hypothesis.** Sites with a lower C:N ratio (more available nitrogen) have a
higher LUE, because more nitrogen allows more photosynthetic capacity per leaf.

**Method.** Topsoil C:N is the ratio of soil organic carbon to total nitrogen
from SoilGrids, thickness-weighted over 0–30 cm. LUE is the sum of daily GPP
(g C m⁻² d⁻¹) divided by the sum of daily incoming shortwave radiation
SW_IN_F (MJ m⁻² d⁻¹) over the three months with the highest mean GPP at each
site. Leaf nitrogen per mass from PlantTraits is shown as a second possible
link between soil and photosynthesis.

```{r q-data}
# Topsoil 0–30 cm, gewichtet nach Schichtdicke
soil_top <- soil |>
  filter(top_cm < 30) |>
  mutate(w = bottom_cm - top_cm) |>
  summarise(value = weighted.mean(mean, w), .by = c(site_id, property)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = property, values_from = value) |>
  mutate(CN = soc / nitrogen)

# Tageswerte
daily <- all_hh |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(time)) |>
  summarise(GPP = mean(GPP) * 1.0378,       # g C m⁻² d⁻¹
            SW  = mean(SW_IN_F) * 0.0864,   # MJ m⁻² d⁻¹
            .by = c(site, date)) |>
  mutate(month = as.integer(format(date, "%m")))

# Die drei Monate mit der höchsten mittleren GPP
peak <- daily |>
  summarise(gpp_month = mean(GPP, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(site, month)) |>
  group_by(site) |>
  slice_max(gpp_month, n = 3) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(site, month)

# Lichtnutzungseffizienz
lue <- daily |>
  semi_join(peak, by = c("site", "month")) |>
  filter(!is.na(GPP), !is.na(SW)) |>
  summarise(LUE         = sum(GPP) / sum(SW),
            n_days      = n(),
            peak_months = paste(sort(unique(month)), collapse = ", "),
            .by = site) |>
  rename(site_id = site)

q <- lue |>
  left_join(soil_top |> select(site_id, soc, nitrogen, CN), by = "site_id") |>
  left_join(traits |> select(site_id, leaf_N_mass, leaf_N_mass_aoa), by = "site_id") |>
  arrange(CN)

q |>
  select(Site = site_id,
         `SOC (g kg⁻¹)` = soc, `N (g kg⁻¹)` = nitrogen, `C:N (–)` = CN,
         `Leaf N (mg g⁻¹)` = leaf_N_mass, `Leaf N AOA` = leaf_N_mass_aoa,
         `Peak months` = peak_months, `Days` = n_days,
         `LUE (g C MJ⁻¹)` = LUE) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```
The PlantTraits area-of-applicability flag (`_aoa`) is 0 for all traits at all
five towers. It is not yet clear whether 0 means inside or outside the area of
applicability; the leaf N values should therefore be read with caution.
```{r q-figure}
#| fig-cap: "Peak-season light-use efficiency against topsoil C:N (SoilGrids, 0–30 cm) and community leaf nitrogen (PlantTraits). n = 5 towers."
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 9
q |>
  select(site_id, LUE,
         `Topsoil C:N (-)` = CN,
         `Leaf N (mg/g)` = leaf_N_mass) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(site_id, LUE), names_to = "driver") |>
  ggplot(aes(value, LUE, label = site_id)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(size = 3.5, box.padding = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ driver, scales = "free_x", strip.position = "bottom") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.15)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.15)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = expression("Peak-season LUE (g C MJ"^-1*")")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(strip.placement = "outside")
```

The figure does not support the hypothesis. BR-Ma2 shows the highest LUE,
although it has the second-highest C:N ratio (about 13). The lowest LUE, in
contrast, occurs at IT-Tor, which also has the highest C:N ratio (about 15).
Both the low LUE and the high soil carbon content at IT-Tor can be explained
by the characteristics of this alpine site: the short growing season and low
temperatures limit photosynthesis as well as the microbial decomposition of
organic matter, so carbon accumulates in the soil. It is therefore likely that
any nitrogen signal is masked by more dominant climate controls.
With only five towers (n = 5) in very different climates, this comparison is
descriptive and cannot test a statistical relationship; differences in
vegetation type, management (e.g. fertilisation at the US-UiB cropland) and
partitioning method (DT at BR-Ma2, NT elsewhere) may also affect LUE.
In addition, the low soil carbon, low C:N and high pH (8.4) at CN-Zha suggest
that the 250 m SoilGrids pixel represents the surrounding dry soils rather
than the wetland itself. Testing the hypothesis properly would require more
towers within a similar climate, for example using the data of the whole class.
